analysis.one_liner: Repeals the legal immunity shielding phone and internet companies that helped warrantless government surveillance.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on September 29, 2009 and received no further action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2008, Congress gave phone and internet companies retroactive legal immunity for participating in the Terrorist Surveillance Program, a warrantless wiretapping effort that swept in Americans' calls and emails. This bill would have deleted that immunity, meaning customers whose communications were collected could sue the companies. It never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary Americans whose phone calls, emails, and internet records were collected without warrants would have regained the ability to sue the telecommunications companies that handed over their data, and the courts could have held those companies accountable. It also would have re-established the principle that private companies must see a lawful warrant before turning over customer records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Customers whose communications were warrantlessly collected

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes Title VIII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the section added by the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 that grants retroactive immunity protection to electronic communication service providers that participated in the Terrorist Surveillance Program.

Removing that protection would have restored the right of private citizens to bring civil suits against telephone and wireless companies that turned over customer records without a warrant, instead of having those lawsuits shut down by statute.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the large telecommunications companies that participated in the program would have faced the cost of defending and potentially settling lawsuits, and any litigation could have forced disclosure of details of intelligence programs in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Phone and internet companies with immunity

drawbacks.text: The 2008 immunity was written precisely so that companies that acted on government assurances could not be held liable for cooperation with intelligence programs; repealing it would have exposed those companies to years of litigation over conduct the government itself directed.
Civil suits challenging the surveillance program risked drawing classified program details into open court, a concern national security officials raised when the immunity was first enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit was accountability: citizens whose communications were collected without a warrant would have had their day in court against the companies that facilitated the program. The cost falls on the companies, and some of the litigation could have disclosed sensitive intelligence practices. The immunity at issue, however, already cut off those suits in 2008, so the bill's main effect would have been restoring a legal remedy that ordinary people lost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the Retroactive Immunity Repeal Act on September 29, 2009, with Feingold, Leahy, and Merkley as the other sponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; that is the last action ever taken on it.
The committee held no hearing or vote on the bill, it never reached the Senate floor, and no version was ever considered in the House before the 111th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large telecommunications providers that received retroactive immunity under the 2008 FISA Amendments Act are better off: the statute shielding them from customer lawsuits remains on the books, untouched. Americans who wanted their day in court over the warrantless surveillance program got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the telecom retroactive immunity provisions.

for.name: Sens. Russell Feingold, Patrick Leahy, and Jeff Merkley

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held: support came only from four of the Senate's 58 Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on, but the bill died in committee without any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Telecommunications providers (phone, wireless, and internet companies)
industries.note: The bill would have struck the 2008 provision that shields these companies from civil suits for turning over customer records to the Terrorist Surveillance Program. Because the bill died, that immunity stands and customers whose data was warrantlessly collected have no recourse against the companies.
